Mishnah opening “Perek Kirah”: kirah and kupach were movable earthenware stoves with mouth upward; kirah fits two pots, kupach one, so kupach retains more heat than kirah but less than a tannur. A tannur is fixed to the ground, narrow above and wide below so its heat concentrates more than kirah/kupach; it is the bakers’ oven where bread was stuck to the walls. Ran writes that R. Chananel held our side-opening ovens have the same law as a kirah.

Regarding fuel of olive-residue/wood: since stirring helps for the night meal, if it cooked somewhat erev Shabbat we fear he will stir — specifically once it reached one-third cooking; less than one-third is treated as “raw” and may be left. The Tur here treats maachal ben derosa as one-third (Rashi) not half (Rambam); he chose stringency for Shabbat. In YD 69 (blood) he used “half-roasted” as a separate stringency; in YD 113 (bishul akum) he was lenient since it is rabbinic.

“Or it was raw, not cooked at all”: Shabbat 18a permits placing a completely raw pot near dark because it won’t be eaten tonight, so he removes his mind and will not stir. Some (a Tosafos approach) wanted to distinguish tannur (strong heat) from kirah (air controls, stirring concern), but our author explains the major view permits even on a kirah: either because the Gemara’s girsa is “permitted” without “in a tannur,” or because “in a tannur” is stated as a greater novelty. Semag/Semak similarly permit on a kirah and even in a tannur. And if it is mitztamek vera lo, it is certainly permitted (no reason to stir).

“Unless he raked”: meaning he removed all coals. Ran’s explanation (decreeing due to great retained heat) is rejected here; rather, “garuf” is not “swept to the side,” but fully removed for a kirah. In a Gemara-era tannur we are stringent: forbidden even if coals were removed.

“But to lean near it”: Gemara asks whether leaning is permitted. Tosafos explain the question is in an un-garuf case and depends whether the Mishnah is about leaving or returning; they conclude leaning is permitted. However, they add one cannot prove from this to leaning right next to an open fire, since here the kirah’s wall separates. Yet Sefer HaTerumah (231), Semag, Semak, Hagahos Maimoniyos, and Maharam permit leaning a pot near a fire even near dark, comparing to meat on coals once roasted maachal ben derosa, and to a raw pot placed near coals. From Rosh’s discussion of placing a water-jar near a fire, it seems one may lean somewhat near the fire (even on Shabbat) with a clear offset that provides a hekker; but placing a pot directly on coals, touching them, is certainly forbidden for the Rif view (all the more so than leaving on a kirah). Practices to leave pots on coals until returning from synagogue rely on Chanania (Rashi/R. Yona) and treat it as “leaving,” not “insulation.”

Kupach: the Tur wrote that a kupach is “like a kirah” and is permitted with garuf u’ketum; Beis Yosef objected since with straw/hay there are no coals to stir. The explanation: a baraisa (supporting Abaye, and halacha follows Abaye) says: a kupach fueled with straw/hay — one may lean but not place on top; thus the Mishnah’s “like a kirah” must be in a garuf u’ketum case (as Rav Ada b. Ahava establishes), while the baraisa is in a non-garuf case. Hence kupach is an intermediate: stricter than kirah, lenient compared to tannur. With wood/residue it is treated like tannur; with straw/hay it can be treated stricter than kirah but lenient compared to tannur. And in cases where no stirring concern exists (raw / mitztamek vera lo), we do not differentiate among kirah/kupach/tannur.

Rif vs Rashi/R. Yona: Rif reads the Mishnah as about leaving (and rules like the Rabbis) — forbidden to leave on a kirah fueled with residue/wood until garuf or ketum — unlike Chanania. Rashi/R. Yona read the Mishnah as about returning: returning requires garuf/ketum, but leaving is permitted even if not garuf/ketum — like Chanania. The Rishonim discuss proofs at length. The reason returning is forbidden: we decree returning erev Shabbat near dark lest one return on Shabbat. Where there was still time to reboil if it had cooled, that is treated like “leaving,” not “returning.” Returning is permitted on a garuf/ketum kirah because that provides a hekker.

Tannur: from “tannur even garuf u’ketum one may not return” it implies the prohibition is specifically return, while leaving might be permitted even in a non-garuf tannur (per Razah and Tosafos under the “returning” reading). But Semag/Semak hold: even if halacha follows Chanania for a kirah, a tannur’s stronger heat makes it stricter, so leaving in a tannur is forbidden unless garuf/ketum. They bring support from the “raw pot” sugya and “cooked/not-cooked” language, reading it about a tannur. We are stringent in Shabbat matters.

Kupach again: the Tur’s distinction (straw/hay: requires garuf for “returning” or for “leaving,” depending on how one reads the sugya) is grounded in that baraisa; the Rif reading will treat it as distinctions in leaving; Rashi/R. Yona as distinctions in returning.

“All this is for leaving for the night”: Beis Yosef questioned whether “night” is literal. Sefer HaTerumah (231) writes that plain “leaving” is for the night; if for tomorrow, it is evident he is not concerned to heat it further, so no stirring fear — but this is discussed within the Chanania/Rabbis frameworks. The Tur used “night” as the normal case; for tomorrow people more commonly use insulation. Claims that “for tomorrow” permits even in a non-garuf case are not supported; in a non-garuf case (per Rabbis) there is no distinction between night and tomorrow in “leaving.”

“This leaving is not insulation”: Rosh wrote so. Beis Yosef explained “insulation on coals” as when the pot’s bottom touches coals; our author argues from the Gemara that insulation is when the pot is covered. Here “insulation on coals” means the pot is packed around with cloth/rags and set above (on stones) with coals below; “leaving” is when the pot is uncovered and set above stones with coals below. Insulation is stricter: even fully cooked is forbidden (decree lest one insulate in embers and stir), as Rosh cites R. Tam — unlike Rashbam who equates insulation to leaving. Sefer HaTerumah and Ran present this as Rashi’s approach, but our author maintains Rashi also agrees insulation is stricter; “adds heat” was used to explain why residue/wood is stricter than straw/hay (stirring can keep adding heat), while garuf/ketum supplies a hekker.

“Anything forbidden to leave…”: Gemara 38a: one forgot a pot on a kirah and it cooked on Shabbat — the Sages penalized even the forgetful (because people were leaving intentionally and claiming “we forgot”). Tosafos/Rosh read the question to apply even under Chanania when it did not reach maachal ben derosa, and under Rabbis even when it did. A second question: “transgressed and left” — is there a penalty? It is discussed via R. Yosei’s case of dried eggs. Our author explains the Tur’s strictness, but for halacha: most understand the penalty applies to the one who left it, not to others, because “a person does not sin so others benefit”; the plain Shulchan Aruch wording also implies “for him” only.

Rambam’s distinction in “forgot”: he rules the first case strictly as a penalty (unintentional like intentional), but in the case of fully cooked mitztamek vi’yafeh lo, the Gemara’s question remains unresolved and we are lenient — specifically if it was forgotten, not done intentionally. The Tur objected “why distinguish,” arguing the Gemara compares “transgressed and left” to “forgot.” The author here offers reconciliations, including that Rif’s version implies leniency even for intentional in mitztamek vi’yafeh lo; and that the discussion is rabbinic doubt. Practically: many are lenient for mitztamek vi’yafeh lo even if intentionally left (rabbinic doubt), but if one intentionally did so, it is at least forbidden for that Shabbat and should not be repeated.

Seif 2: A garuf u’ketum kirah — Beis Hillel permit removing and returning. The Gemara teaches that returning is permitted even on Shabbat. The Tur’s phrasing implies: specifically if he removed it on Shabbat he may return; but if he removed it erev Shabbat, returning on Shabbat is forbidden per Tosafos, whereas Ran (from Yerushalmi) permits; the common practice is lenient. “As long as it is boiling” implies: even if still warm, it is forbidden unless actually boiling; otherwise it is like placing initially on Shabbat. If fully cooled, it is obviously forbidden due to cooking, as in siman 318.

“Only on its back (not inside)”: Gemara 37a: permitted on top, forbidden inside. Rashi explains “inside” is real insulation in embers; thus “inside” means the pot is fully within the cavity sitting on the floor. If the pot’s bottom fills the mouth area, it is still called “on top.” This matches Rashi’s language about the usual placement on the rim or on a cover, contrary to Beis Yosef’s reading.

Regarding returning near dark on a non-garuf kirah: Beis Yosef’s explanation (“when not fully cooked we don’t decree because it would be Shabbat cooking”) is challenged. Rather, Rosh’s intent is: when it is still in the middle of cooking, people commonly remove/return several times erev Shabbat, and the Shabbat return case is generally about already-cooked pots kept warm; therefore forbidding erev-Shabbat return here would be a “decree on a decree.” By contrast, a fully cooked pot left on the kirah solely to preserve heat resembles Shabbat return, so the decree applies. Although returning on Shabbat is forbidden even when boiling (for stirring concern), that is not because of cooking but because of stirring without a hekker; garuf/ketum supplies a hekker. The Tur’s allowance for returning on Shabbat in a garuf/ketum case is only when fully cooked; otherwise it would be real cooking.

He reiterates: a pot not fully cooked (even if it reached maachal ben derosa) may be returned erev Shabbat on a non-garuf kirah, even when there is not time to reboil if it cooled; the Rishonim disagree (Sefer HaTerumah/Semag/Semak/Hagahos Maimoniyos forbid). It is difficult to reconcile the Mishnah with Rosh/Tur on this point, but if the dish is completely raw or one inserted a raw piece, all agree one may return it erev Shabbat (no decree, since it’s clearly not for immediate eating).

Tannur: the Tur reads that whenever return is allowed on a kirah (Shabbat or erev Shabbat), it is forbidden on a Gemara-era tannur even if garuf/ketum. Thus, a pot not fully cooked (but maachal ben derosa) that might be returnable erev Shabbat on a kirah is still forbidden to return in a tannur. However, with a completely raw dish or a raw limb inserted, even a tannur may be returned erev Shabbat (no decree). The Maggid Mishneh and others who forbid even raw/mitztamek vera in a tannur refer specifically to returning on Shabbat, not to erev-Shabbat return; still, in the erev-Shabbat “returning” decree approach, the boundaries are not fully clear and require care.
